## 3. How to use these documents

### If you have 10 minutes
Read `Project_Presentation.pptx` slides 11–15 (findings, the three Critical
items, the High-severity items, and the Phase 1 plan), then slide 18 (the seven
decisions needed from the business).

### If you are the business sponsor
1. `BRD.md` §1 — executive summary.
2. `BRD.md` §2.3 — **the inferred objectives. Confirm or correct these.** They
   are the only statement of purpose in the document that did not come from the
   code, and every proposed KPI target depends on them.
3. `BRD.md` §15 — the 15 open questions. **OQ-13 (how sensitive is this data)
   determines whether the Critical findings are urgent remediation or planned
   work.**
4. `BRD.md` §16 — risks, and §22 — the sign-off template.

### If you are the technical owner
1. `Project_Audit_Report.md` §6.1 limitation 2 and §6.2 UQ-01 — **verify first
   whether the live database's policies match `schema.sql`.** That single
   answer sets the severity of the three Critical findings.
2. `Project_Audit_Report.md` §3 — the findings, in severity order.
3. `Project_Audit_Report.md` §4 — the prioritised backlog, 36 actions in three
   phases with effort bands.
4. `BRD.md` §21 — the traceability matrix, to see what is and is not covered by
   a test.

### If you are running UAT
`BRD.md` §17.2 — 30 scenarios with steps, expected results and the requirements
each verifies. **Six are written to fail against the current build**
(UAT-09, UAT-13, UAT-20, UAT-21, UAT-22, UAT-30). That is deliberate: run them
today to confirm the findings, and re-run them after Phase 1 to confirm the
fixes. Prerequisites are listed at the head of §17.2.

### If you are presenting
Every slide has speaker notes carrying the supporting repository evidence —
file paths and line numbers — and the caveats that belong with that slide. Open
the deck in PowerPoint and use Presenter View. The deck is fully editable:
native tables and text boxes, no images, no embedded objects.

## 4. How to regenerate

All build inputs live in `.presentation-build/`, which is outside this folder so
that `deliverables/` holds only documents.

```powershell
cd C:\Users\User\Documents\procurement-tracker

# BRD.docx  — from BRD.md, via Word automation
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .presentation-build\md-to-docx.ps1 `
  -InputFile deliverables\BRD.md `
  -OutputFile deliverables\BRD.docx `
  -DocTitle 'Business Requirements Document - New Model Procurement Tracker'

# Project_Presentation.pptx + .pdf  — from audit-slides.json, via PowerPoint automation
powershell -NoProfile -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .presentation-build\create-deck.ps1 `
  -DataFile audit-slides.json `
  -OutputName Project_Presentation `
  -PreviewFolder audit-preview
```

| Input | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `.presentation-build/md-to-docx.ps1` | Markdown → DOCX. Handles headings, pipe tables, lists, fenced code, blockquotes and inline formatting. Written for this exercise. |
| `.presentation-build/audit-slides.json` | The deck's content: 20 slides with section, title, body, caption and speaker notes. Edit this, not the PPTX, if the deck needs changing. |
| `.presentation-build/create-deck.ps1` | JSON → PPTX + PDF + slide PNGs. **Pre-existing**, used for the three November decks. This exercise made one additive change: the cover slide now reads `eyebrow`, `title`, `subtitle` and `footer` from the data file, falling back to the original literals when those keys are absent — which they are in the three earlier slide files, so those decks build unchanged. (Not re-run to confirm; the fallback is a plain `if` on each key.) |
| `.presentation-build/audit-preview/slide-NN.png` | Rendered preview of every slide, used to check for clipped or overflowing content. |
| `.presentation-build/layout-check.txt` | Automated text-box overflow report. Written only when the build finds warnings; the last build reported 0, so no file is present. |

**Requirements:** Microsoft Word and PowerPoint (COM automation; both confirmed
present as version 16.0). No npm packages, Python libraries or network access
are needed. Neither script reads or writes anything in `src/`, `supabase/` or
any `.sql` file.

## 6. Limitations you must know before acting on these documents

1. **Almost nothing was verified at runtime.** No Supabase project, no deployed
   instance and no browser session were available. Apart from `npm run check`
   and `npm run build`, everything is static analysis. Statements about
   concurrency outcomes, row-level-security effects, email delivery and
   accessibility in practice are inferences from code and SQL. The BRD labels
   each requirement accordingly, and the audit report states a confidence level
   per finding.

2. **The reproduction steps for the three Critical findings were not executed.**
   They are derived from the code and schema. Confirm them in a controlled
   environment before treating them as demonstrated.

3. **It is unknown whether the live database matches the committed schema.** If
   someone has tightened the row-level-security policies since `schema.sql` was
   written, AUD-001 to AUD-003 change severity. This is unresolved question
   UQ-01 and it is the single most important thing to check first.

4. **No business stakeholder was consulted.** Every objective, benefit, KPI
   target, severity, likelihood and priority is either inferred from code or
   proposed by this audit. Nothing has been confirmed by an owner. Proposed
   benefits are labelled as proposals throughout and must not be presented as
   measured results.

5. **Credentials were not inspected.** `.env.local` exists in the project root
   and was deliberately never opened. No credential, token, key or private value
   appears anywhere in these deliverables.

6. **Excluded from line-by-line review:** `node_modules/`, `dist/` (build
   output, regenerated by the build check and git-ignored), `package-lock.json`,
   binary preview images, and the six pre-existing PPTX/PDF files in this
   folder. The CSS block in `src/App.jsx` (lines 908–1201) was reviewed for the
   behaviours that carry requirements — responsive breakpoints, theming,
   reduced-motion, focus and disabled states — rather than property by property.

## 7. Open decisions

Nothing in this document set has been approved. The sign-off block in
`BRD.md` §22 is an unsigned template for a review that has not taken place.

Four decisions gate everything else:

| | Decision | Who | Why it is first |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | **UQ-01** — do the live database policies match `schema.sql`? | Technical owner | Sets the severity of all three Critical findings |
| 2 | **OQ-13** — how commercially sensitive is this data? | MD | Sets their urgency: remediation or planned work |
| 3 | **OQ-10** — how is the application actually deployed today? | Maintainer | Nothing can be safely remediated until the release path is known |
| 4 | **OQ-01** — where did the 100/85/75/60/25/0 day schedule come from? | Procurement lead | Determines whether any delay figure or late count is meaningful |

The remaining eleven business questions are in `BRD.md` §15; the remaining seven
technical questions are in `Project_Audit_Report.md` §6.2.

---

## 8. Headline assessment

The workflow engine is well built — one gate function for every stage change,
nothing derived is stored, the optimistic lock is correct, and the interface
refuses to claim a save before the write lands.

The security model does not exist. The application has no server of its own, so
every rule it enforces runs in a place the user controls, while the key shipped
to that user grants unrestricted access to the database. `README.md` in the
project root says so plainly, which is to the author's credit — but documenting
a gap is not closing it.

For a small, trusted, internal team working on data that would be inconvenient
rather than damaging to lose, the system does its job and does the hard parts of
it well. It should not be the sole record of anything, and should not hold
commercially sensitive data, until Phase 1 of the backlog is complete. Five of
the eight Phase 1 items are under a day each.
